description: Distinct engineering memories with same-domain distractors and disjoint calibration/evaluation targets. MindLeak lessons are paraphrased from tracked documentation, not exported from a live memory database.

sources.note: Paraphrased lessons and adapted negative controls. These describe MindLeak proper, not Light. Historical benchmark scores are not labels for this corpus.
All other project facts are fictional. No personal memories, credentials, or runtime exports.

memories.text: MindLeak proper performs execution, Git, and syntax-tree ingestion deterministically without LLM token use.
MindLeak proper confines generative model calls to its asynchronous consolidation layer.
MindLeak proper coordinates agents cooperatively rather than preemptively.
MindLeak proper does not sandbox agent processes or prevent their filesystem writes.
MindLeak proper's Memory Plane is a decay-weighted structural and episodic context graph.
Lodestar is MindLeak proper's Intent Plane for durable goals, designs, coordination, knowledge, and proof.
MindLeak proper computes effective edge weights at query time rather than persisting decayed weights.
MindLeak proper keeps its consolidation model optional so deterministic ingestion does not depend on model availability.
MindLeak proper's consolidation provider uses an OpenAI-compatible chat completions endpoint.
GraphStore owns graph reads and writes in MindLeak proper.
MindLeak proper keeps shared path normalization and short-hash helpers in its ingestion module.
An unknown file ID in MindLeak proper means the graph has not observed it, not that nothing depends on it.
MindLeak proper's deterministic Rust impact traversal stops at the crate boundary.
MindLeak proper's impact traversal prefers under-reporting missing evidence to guessing dependencies.
MindLeak proper's documented default work-claim lease became 1800 seconds on 2026-08-26.
Ordinary file edits and builds do not by themselves renew MindLeak proper's Lodestar claim heartbeat.
A same-owner reclaim in MindLeak proper preserves the evidence window while recording a lease lapse.
MindLeak proper requires explicit path staging for scoped commits instead of staging a mixed worktree wholesale.
MindLeak proper assigns separate worktrees and branches to concurrent workstreams.
MindLeak proper uses patch equivalence from git cherry to check whether rewritten work landed upstream.
MindLeak proper requires a bug regression to fail before its fix and pass afterward.
MindLeak proper does not treat a quiet impact query as proof that a file has no dependents.
MindLeak's July 2026 recall experiments found overlapping similarity distributions for real and nonsense queries.
MindLeak's 2026-07-31 grounding benchmark rejected all seven control queries but returned relevant results for only five of seven real queries.
Cedar uses PostgreSQL 17 for its primary relational database.
Cedar database tests require a disposable database with a name ending in _test.
Cedar uses SQL migrations numbered with four-digit prefixes.
Cedar exposes its local database on port 55432.
Cedar serves its local memory endpoint on port 8088.
Cedar sets its database connection pool maximum to eight connections.
Cedar gives each SQL statement a fifteen-second execution budget.
Cedar aborts database lock acquisition after five seconds.
Cedar stores original memory text without rewriting it.
Cedar commits source text and all derived fragments in one database transaction.
Cedar stores missing embeddings as SQL NULL values.
Cedar refuses to mix embedding dimensions in an existing database.
Cedar uses a GIN index for English full-text recall.
Cedar backs up its database daily at 02:00 UTC.
Cedar retains daily database backups for fourteen days.
Cedar recovery drills restore backups into a separate database.
Cedar requires TLS verification for remote database connections.
Cedar does not automatically erase stored memories with age.
Cedar prevents memory text from appearing in application logs.
Cedar limits each raw memory to 32768 UTF-8 bytes.
Cedar rejects a memory decomposition containing more than 64 fragments.
Cedar serializes schema initialization with a transaction-scoped advisory lock.
Cedar allows at most fifty fragments in one recall response.
Cedar treats caller-supplied agent identifiers as provenance rather than tenant authentication.
Maple uses PostgreSQL 16 for its payment ledger.
Maple stores payment amounts as integer minor units rather than floating-point values.
Maple requires an idempotency key on payment creation requests.
Maple retains payment idempotency keys for twenty-four hours.
Maple serves its local payment API on port 9090.
Maple exposes its local ledger database on port 55434.
Maple rejects webhook signatures older than five minutes.
Maple retries failed webhook delivery at most six times.
Maple caps exponential webhook retry backoff at fifteen minutes.
Maple does not retry a declined card authorization automatically.
Maple requires two approvals for changes to settlement code.
Maple's default settlement currency is GBP.
Maple runs settlement reconciliation daily at 04:30 UTC.
Maple routes duplicate provider events through the existing ledger entry.
Maple stores payment provider event timestamps in UTC.
Maple refunds cannot exceed the uncancelled captured amount.
Maple separates live and sandbox provider credentials.
Maple never persists raw card security codes.
Maple redacts authorization headers from request logs.
Maple retains audit events for seven years.
Maple requires a manual review before releasing held settlements.
Maple integration tests use simulated payment providers.
Maple's ledger permits only balanced double-entry postings.
Maple reports a payment as successful only after the ledger transaction commits.
Lumen builds its web client with React 19.
Lumen uses TypeScript strict mode for application code.
Lumen runs its development server on port 5173.
Lumen uses Playwright for browser workflow tests.
Lumen runs component unit tests with Vitest rather than Node's built-in runner.
Lumen formats displayed dates in the user's selected time zone.
Lumen keeps unsaved form edits when a background refresh completes.
Lumen requires an explicit confirmation before deleting a saved workspace.
Lumen cancels an obsolete search request when a newer query replaces it.
Lumen debounces search input for 250 milliseconds.
Lumen requires accessible names for icon-only buttons.
Lumen requires keyboard focus to return to the trigger when a dialog closes.
Lumen disables decorative motion when reduced-motion preferences are enabled.
Lumen renders error details next to the corresponding invalid field.
Lumen does not store session tokens in browser localStorage.
Lumen serves font files from its own origin.
Lumen's production content security policy forbids inline scripts.
Lumen labels monetary values with their currency code.
Lumen tests layouts at a minimum viewport width of 320 pixels.
Lumen preserves table sort order when switching pagination pages.
Lumen displays empty-state rows instead of fabricated sample records.
Lumen keeps image dimensions reserved while images load.
Lumen excludes source maps from public production assets.
Lumen renders untrusted Markdown without enabling raw HTML.
Nimbus listens for local HTTPS traffic on port 8443.
Nimbus exposes its metrics endpoint on port 9100.
Nimbus uses TLS 1.3 for external client connections.
Nimbus requires mutual TLS between internal gateway instances.
Nimbus verifies upstream certificate hostnames.
Nimbus rejects requests with conflicting Content-Length headers.
Nimbus accepts forwarded client IP headers only from configured trusted proxies.
Nimbus limits incoming JSON request bodies to one mebibyte.
Nimbus gives upstream connection attempts a three-second timeout.
Nimbus gives upstream responses a thirty-second timeout.
Nimbus returns HTTP 429 when a client's rate limit is exhausted.
Nimbus allows a burst of twenty requests per client.
Nimbus does not retry non-idempotent upstream requests without an idempotency key.
Nimbus drains established connections for up to thirty seconds during shutdown.
Nimbus rotates server certificates without restarting listener sockets.
Nimbus logs request IDs instead of complete request bodies.
Nimbus strips credentials before forwarding cross-origin redirects.
Nimbus disables cross-origin browser access unless an origin is explicitly allowlisted.
Nimbus includes a Retry-After header with rate-limit responses.
Nimbus separates readiness checks from liveness checks.
Nimbus does not expose stack traces in public error responses.
Nimbus loads its upstream routing table atomically.
Nimbus leaves an existing routing table active when a replacement fails validation.
Nimbus caches successful DNS resolutions for sixty seconds.
Orion uses nomic-embed-text-v1.5 as its embedding model.
Orion stores embedding vectors with 768 dimensions.
Orion sends up to thirty-two texts in one embedding request.
Orion preserves input order when reconstructing indexed embedding responses.
Orion rejects embeddings containing non-finite values.
Orion rejects zero-length embedding vectors.
Orion records the model checksum beside each benchmark result.
Orion treats cosine similarity as a ranking signal rather than a probability of truth.
Orion calibrates relevance thresholds using development queries rather than held-out evaluation queries.
Orion leaves language-model extraction disabled for already-atomic facts.
Orion gives local embedding requests a ten-second timeout.
Orion gives optional chat extraction requests a forty-five-second timeout.
Orion rejects chat responses that end because the output-token limit was reached.
Orion requires structured JSON-schema output from chat extraction providers.
Orion preserves negation when extracting factual claims.
Orion does not resolve a pronoun when its subject is absent from the source.
Orion stores an immutable source record alongside extracted facts.
Orion does not silently switch to sentence splitting when an enabled chat provider fails.
Orion pins its tokenizer revision for reproducible embedding evaluation.
Orion runs approximate-neighbour accuracy checks against an exact-search reference.
Orion deduplicates identical fragment IDs before fusing retrieval rankings.
Orion evaluates unanswered questions separately from answerable-query recall.
Orion keeps warm-request latency separate from model-loading time.
Orion requires a new vector index when the embedding model changes.
Atlas builds Rust packages with a locked dependency graph.
Atlas publishes separate Linux binaries for x86_64 and aarch64.
Atlas publishes separate macOS binaries for Intel and Apple Silicon.
Atlas runs PostgreSQL integration tests against a disposable database ending in _test.
Atlas treats Clippy warnings as build failures.
Atlas requires formatting checks before merge.
Atlas validates repository documentation links in CI.
Atlas uses Node.js 22 for dependency-free repository scripts.
Atlas does not run Vitest test files with node --test.
Atlas rejects duplicate architecture-decision record numbers.
Atlas creates release notes from per-change changelog fragments.
Atlas release jobs require an explicit version tag.
Atlas leaves new releases in draft state until a maintainer approves them.
Atlas computes SHA-256 checksums for every release archive.
Atlas refuses publication when the tag version differs from the package version.
Atlas pins container base images by immutable digest.
Atlas keys its dependency cache with the lockfile hash.
Atlas runs Linux, Windows, and macOS jobs independently.
Atlas excludes credentials from uploaded failure artifacts.
Atlas installs pre-commit and pre-push hooks during contributor setup.
Atlas requires proof that regression tests failed before their fixes.
Atlas never marks database tests as passed when their feature flag was disabled.
Atlas limits cross-compilation code generation to one job in its small container runner.
Atlas requires an explicit opt-in before promoting a container image to the latest tag.
Vega stores persistent database files in a named container volume.
Vega keeps its bundled PostgreSQL listener on a Unix socket only.
Vega performs incremental backups every six hours.
Vega retains incremental backups for thirty days.
Vega tests restoring backups on the first Monday of each month.
Vega's recovery point objective is six hours.
Vega's recovery time objective is ninety minutes.
Vega does not remove persistent volumes during an ordinary shutdown.
Vega verifies that container recreation preserves previously written records.
Vega requires bearer authentication on its exposed HTTP endpoint.
Vega reads production secrets from mounted secret files.
Vega rotates its service token during a scheduled maintenance window.
Vega limits database disk use alerts to the operations notification channel.
Vega warns when database storage exceeds eighty percent of its allocated capacity.
Vega restarts failed service processes under Supervisor.
Vega gives graceful application shutdown twenty seconds before termination.
Vega tests the packaged executable rather than a source-tree substitute.
Vega uses the Docker image format when building Podman images that need HEALTHCHECK metadata.
Vega does not publish database ports in its all-in-one deployment.
Vega verifies TLS trust before sending production requests.
Vega retains the original failure log when a deployment retry succeeds.
Vega requires an operator to authorize destructive database cleanup.
Vega tests IPv4 and IPv6 loopback connectivity independently.
Vega records the deployed binary checksum in its operations inventory.
Pulse supports MCP over stdio for native local clients.
Pulse supports authenticated Streamable HTTP for remote MCP clients.
Pulse reserves stdio stdout exclusively for MCP protocol messages.
Pulse sends diagnostic messages to stderr.
Pulse uses the official MCP SDK rather than implementing JSON-RPC framing itself.
Pulse waits for the MCP initialization handshake before listing tools.
Pulse checks the server's advertised capabilities rather than assuming requested capabilities were granted.
Pulse treats recalled memory text as untrusted data rather than executable instructions.
Pulse passes agent provenance filters on every project-scoped memory query.
Pulse closes its MCP transport when a command completes.
Pulse uses a fresh agent namespace for each benchmark invocation.
Pulse emits benchmark JSON on stdout and progress on stderr.
Pulse rejects a benchmark database URL that does not name a disposable _test database.
Pulse does not include memory text or provider response bodies in benchmark reports.
Pulse records the corpus hash and binary hash in each benchmark report.
Pulse fails a benchmark run when recall returns a memory from another namespace.
Pulse gives duplicate source memories relevance credit only once per ranking.
Pulse keeps duplicate result slots occupied when calculating ranking metrics.
Pulse averages recall equally across answerable queries rather than weighting by their number of labels.
Pulse reports an absent metric population as null rather than a perfect score.
Pulse records benchmark failures separately from measured retrieval misses.
Pulse excludes unanswerable questions from mean reciprocal rank calculations.
Pulse validates structured tool results before assigning retrieval scores.
Pulse requires the same corpus and result limit when comparing benchmark configurations.
